Day 1-3: Audit existing content. Document voice attributes.
Day 4-7: Setup Project + first test articles. Iterate voice prompt.
Day 8-14: Roll-out for the team + measurement.

Stage transition: 1→2.
uc-ai-content-ops-launch.mistakes: Doing a UC without voice work. Pipeline without brand voice = AI-generic texts faster, but still generic. Voice setup is 30% of UC time. Do not skip.

ai-native-customer-support.title: AI-Native Customer Support
ai-native-customer-support.what: Customer support teams on AI-native rails: tier-1 automation, agent-assist for tier-2, knowledge base ops, escalation intelligence, quality monitoring, analytics. From «AI answers simple stuff» — to «AI does 70% of the work, humans do the complex».
ai-native-customer-support.why: Support is the most measurable of all transformation directions. Tickets, response time, CSAT, deflection rate — all tracked. ROI is visible in a month. This is the «easy win» for AI in the company.
ai-native-customer-support.when: When tier-1 volume >100 tickets/week. When there is a knowledge base (or capability to build one). When the team is tired of repeat questions and wants to work on complex.
ai-native-customer-support.impact: Deflection rate 0% → 40-60% in 3 months. Tier-2 response time: 2h → 15min (via agent-assist). Agent satisfaction +35% (routine goes away). CSAT holds or grows. Stage 1→3 in 6 months.
ai-native-customer-support.example:
Maturity stages for Support:
Stage 0: Pre-AI — all tickets to humans, average load 50/day/agent.
Stage 1: AI experiments — Claude helps write answers individually.
Stage 2: AI workflows — tier-1 bot closes 30% of requests, agent-assist on tier-2.
Stage 3: AI-native — 60% automation, agents focus on complex cases.
Stage 4: AI-first — proactive support: AI predicts issues before tickets.
ai-native-customer-support.mistakes: Launching AI tier-1 without quality monitoring and escalation. AI will err on 5-15% — without quality monitoring this lands in CSAT. Without escalation, the user gets stuck in a bot loop. Quality + escalation = mandatory from day 1.

cs-tier1.title: AI Tier-1 Automation
cs-tier1.what: Automating first-line support: AI reads incoming ticket → finds answer in knowledge base (RAG) → writes a personalized reply → or escalates to a human. Pipeline with explicit quality gates.
cs-tier1.why: 30-50% of all support tickets are repeat questions (password reset, billing, account access). AI closes this mass with consistent quality. Tier-2 agents focus on complex.
cs-tier1.when: Tier-1 volume >100 tickets/week. Structured knowledge base. Clear FAQ categories (40%+ tickets fit into 20 patterns). Buy-in from CS-lead.
cs-tier1.impact: Deflection: 40-60%. Median response time: 4h → 2min for AI-tickets. Tier-2 load drops by 30-40%. CSAT for AI-tickets: 4.2/5 with right setup (vs 4.4 for humans).
cs-tier1.example:
Tier-1 Workflow:

  Incoming ticket
        ↓
  [Classify intent: FAQ vs complex]
   ├─ FAQ → AI processes with KB
   │         ↓
   │     [Confidence > 0.8?]
   │      ├─ Yes → AI response + log
   │      └─ No  → escalate to tier-2 with AI summary
   └─ Complex → directly to human queue

  Quality gate: 10% random AI responses → human review weekly

Metric: deflection rate weekly, CSAT for AI-tickets.
cs-tier1.mistakes: Doing tier-1 at 80% content. Edge cases accumulate: every AI failure = bad experience. Production rule: AI responds only when confidence is high. Otherwise escalate with AI-prepared context for the human.

cs-agent-assist.title: AI Agent Assist
cs-agent-assist.what: AI as a «co-pilot» for tier-2 agent: real-time response suggestions, autocompletion, similar-case search, template generation. Agent stays in the driver seat, AI accelerates.
cs-agent-assist.why: Agent-assist is less risky than tier-1: human is always in the loop. ROI is faster (response time -50% immediately). Team sees AI as «helper», not «threat». Adoption is much higher.
cs-agent-assist.when: Tier-2/3 team spends time writing responses from scratch. There are historical tickets with good answers. Want to raise velocity without quality loss.
cs-agent-assist.impact: Response time per ticket: 8 min → 3 min. Agents handle 50-70% more tickets/day. Quality consistent (AI used as draft, agent edits). New agent onboarding: -50% (AI compensates junior gap). Stage 1→2.
cs-agent-assist.example:
Agent Assist Setup:

1. Browser plugin or helpdesk integration.
2. Open ticket → AI reads context + customer history.
3. AI suggests:
   - 3 reply variants (formal/friendly/technical)
   - Similar past tickets (resolved)
   - Relevant KB articles
4. Agent selects + edits + sends.
5. AI learns from agent edits (improves suggestions over time).

Real usage: 70% suggestions accepted with minor edits, 20% edited significantly, 10% unused.
cs-agent-assist.mistakes: Forcing agents to use AI «mandatorily». If a suggestion is bad — it forces writing from scratch. Drive adoption through value (show time saved per ticket), not mandate.

cs-knowledge-base.title: AI Knowledge Base Operations
cs-knowledge-base.what: Knowledge base turns from «PDF dump» into a living AI system: vector search, auto-updates based on resolved tickets, gap analysis (what is often asked but no article exists), structured taxonomy.
cs-knowledge-base.why: Without a good KB, all AI support fails. KB = single source of truth for AI. KB quality ≠ article count. Quality KB ops = more impact than just launching AI.
cs-knowledge-base.when: In parallel with tier-1 setup. When AI bot answers «I do not know» to >20% of questions. When agents complain «cannot find the article». When KB has not been updated in >6 months.
cs-knowledge-base.impact: KB findability: 50% → 90% (vector search vs keyword). AI deflection rate grows +15-20% (more coverage). Agent onboarding: -40% time. Stage 1→2.
cs-knowledge-base.example:
KB Ops Pipeline:

Weekly:
  1. AI reads resolved tickets for the week.
  2. Identifies frequent questions without KB articles.
  3. Drafts new KB articles from ticket solutions.
  4. KB editor reviews + publishes.

Monthly:
  1. AI analyzes KB usage (which articles cited).
  2. Flags outdated content (product changed, article did not).
  3. Suggests merges (duplicate articles).

Metric: % of tickets where AI found KB match → up over time.
cs-knowledge-base.mistakes: Making KB only for humans. Modern KB optimization = for AI + humans. Structure (clear headers, atomic articles, metadata) matters for AI retrieval. Otherwise AI does not find — even if the article exists.

cs-escalation.title: AI Escalation Intelligence
cs-escalation.what: Smart escalation: AI decides when to hand off to a human and exactly to whom (by specialization, load, severity). Plus prepares escalation context — the agent gets not «here is a ticket», but «here is a ticket + history + what AI tried».
cs-escalation.why: Dumb escalation = ticket arrives without context, agent spends 5 minutes reading. Smart = agent sees summary + what was already tried + recommended next step. Velocity grows without quality loss.
cs-escalation.when: When tier-1 AI is running and tier-2 routing is needed. When there are specializations (billing vs technical vs account). When escalation is a bottleneck.
cs-escalation.impact: Time-to-resolution for escalated tickets: -40%. Routing accuracy: 80% → 95% (correct specialist on first try). Agent satisfaction +: less «why did they pass this to me».
cs-escalation.example:
Escalation Workflow:

  AI cannot resolve ticket
        ↓
  [Classify problem domain]
   ├─ Billing → queue: billing_team
   ├─ Technical → queue: tech_support
   └─ Account → queue: account_specialists
        ↓
  AI prepares escalation summary:
   - Customer info + history
   - What customer wants
   - What AI tried (and why it didn't work)
   - Suggested next step
        ↓
  Agent picks up: context ready in 30 sec instead of 5 min.

Metric: agent feedback on escalation quality.
cs-escalation.mistakes: Escalating «just in case» at low confidence. If AI errs 10% but escalates 50% — it is degradation. Calibrate threshold: too high = killed deflection, too low = bad quality.

cs-quality-monitoring.title: AI Quality Monitoring
cs-quality-monitoring.what: Continuous monitoring of AI response quality: weekly sample → human review → identify failure patterns → adjust prompts/KB. Without monitoring, AI degrades silently: errors accumulate, no one sees.
cs-quality-monitoring.why: AI is not static: KB changes, product changes, customer questions change. AI that worked in Q1 may slip in Q3. Quality monitoring catches drift before CSAT drops.
cs-quality-monitoring.when: From day 1 of AI tier-1 launch. Mandatory. Not «when there is a problem» — continuous. Minimum: 10% AI responses random sample → weekly review.
cs-quality-monitoring.impact: AI drift detection: before customers notice (CSAT does not drop). Continuous improvement: every week prompts/KB get better. Trust in the AI system grows through explicit quality data. Stage 2→3.
cs-quality-monitoring.example:
Quality Monitoring Process:

Weekly:
  1. Random sample 10% of AI responses.
  2. Quality team rates: accuracy, tone, completeness.
  3. Failure patterns extracted: «AI confuses billing X with Y», «misses context Z».
  4. Action: update KB articles OR adjust system prompt OR add edge case to training data.

Metric:
  - % AI responses rated >4/5
  - Trending direction (better/worse week-over-week)
  - Top 3 failure categories

Escalation: if quality < 4/5 for 2 weeks → pause AI tier-1, investigate.
cs-quality-monitoring.mistakes: Monitoring without action loop. If found errors do not lead to changes — it is theater. Quality monitoring must be embedded in weekly product process (Mon: review, Tue: fix, Wed: validate, ...).

cs-support-analytics.title: AI Support Analytics
cs-support-analytics.what: AI reads support metrics + ticket content → writes insight reports: trending issues, customer sentiment, agent performance patterns, product feedback. Turns support data into product insights.
cs-support-analytics.why: Support is free user research. Thousands of conversations with real customers. But the team drowns in objects/dashboards. AI does the narrative layer + connects to product/marketing teams.
cs-support-analytics.when: Weekly support reviews. When product team wants «voice of customer». When there is a pattern «many complaints about feature X» — need systematic detection.
cs-support-analytics.impact: Time-to-insight: days → hours. Product team gets trending issues automatically. Customer voice loop closes: from ticket → insight → product change → fewer tickets. Stage 2→3.
cs-support-analytics.example:
Weekly Support Analytics Report:

  Inputs:
  - All tickets for the week (resolved + open)
  - CSAT scores + comments
  - Agent performance metrics
  - Product release notes

  AI Output:
  - Top 5 trending issues (with ticket count + delta)
  - Sentiment analysis: where customers are frustrated
  - Correlation: «new feature X released → tickets about X +40%»
  - Recommendations for product team
  - Recommendations for KB updates

Distribution: report shared with product + marketing → closing the loop.
cs-support-analytics.mistakes: Doing support analytics in isolation. If insights do not reach product/engineering — they are useless. Set up explicit channels: weekly «Support Insights» Slack post in #product, monthly review session.

cs-team-workflow.title: AI Customer Support Team Workflow
cs-team-workflow.what: CS team operating model with AI: shared knowledge base ops, common agent-assist setup, AI office hours, quality calibration sessions, AI-aware promotion path for agents. From «AI = a tool» — to «AI = part of how we operate».
cs-team-workflow.why: Individual AI usage in support does not work — consistency for customers is needed (everyone gets same quality answer). Team workflow ensures this through shared setup + processes.
cs-team-workflow.when: When team ≥5 agents use AI. When new agents arrive and «do not know how». When quality is inconsistent between shift teams.
cs-team-workflow.impact: Team velocity: agents process 50%+ more tickets. New agent onboarding: 4 weeks → 2 weeks. Quality consistency across shifts: +60%. AI literacy team-wide.
cs-team-workflow.example:
CS Team Setup:

1. Shared Claude Project «Support Workspace»:
   - KB indexed
   - Brand voice guide (tone for customers)
   - Common scenarios templates

2. CLAUDE.md: response guidelines, escalation criteria, tone rules.

3. Skills: response-drafter, ticket-summarizer, escalation-formatter.

4. Weekly calibration: team reviews 5 AI-handled tickets together. Discusses: what worked, what would change.

5. AI-aware promotion: agents who improve AI workflow → senior path (not just «answer more tickets»).

Result: team functions as a cohesive AI-augmented unit.
cs-team-workflow.mistakes: Treating AI usage as «individual perk». Without team-level workflow, customers get inconsistent experience (depending on which agent picks). AI = team capability, not individual skill.

uc-ai-support-tier1.title: Use Case: Launch AI Tier-1 Support in 3-4 Weeks
uc-ai-support-tier1.what: Full path from «all by hand» to «AI closes 40% of tickets». Cross-layer path through 7 nodes: Foundation → AI Fundamentals → Systems → Transformation.
uc-ai-support-tier1.why: Tier-1 automation = highest-ROI AI project in support. This UC shows a structured approach (not «buy a bot»): KB first, then AI, then quality monitoring.
uc-ai-support-tier1.when: Tier-1 volume >100 tickets/week. Baseline CSAT exists for comparison. Can invest 3-4 weeks in setup. Buy-in from CS-lead AND product (for KB).
uc-ai-support-tier1.impact: Outcome: working tier-1 AI with 40% deflection in 4 weeks. Metrics: deflection rate 0→40%, median response time 4h→2min for AI-tickets, CSAT maintained at baseline.
uc-ai-support-tier1.example:
Path (7 steps):

Week 1: Knowledge Base prep.
1. Foundation: af-rag-basics → understand what RAG needs
2. Foundation: af-vector-db → vector DB choice (pgvector usually enough)
3. Systems: sys-rag-architecture → pattern choice (Advanced RAG mandatory)
4. Audit + restructure existing KB articles

Week 2: AI tier-1 setup.
5. Foundation: prompting → system prompt for support bot
6. Foundation: projects → create «Support Bot» Project with KB
7. Transformation: cs-tier1 → build workflow with quality gates

Week 3: Quality + escalation.
8. Transformation: cs-escalation → correct routing for escalations
9. Transformation: cs-quality-monitoring → setup random sample review

Week 4: Roll-out.
10. Pilot on 1 ticket category. Measure deflection + CSAT.
11. Expand to 3-5 categories. Iterate.

Stage transition: 1→2.
uc-ai-support-tier1.mistakes: Launching AI tier-1 without KB ops first. If the KB is not suitable for AI retrieval (bad structure, outdated) — AI will answer generic or wrong. KB ops = 50% of UC work. Do not skip.

ai-native-product.title: AI-Native Product
ai-native-product.what: Product teams on AI-native rails: discovery research, spec generation, roadmap intelligence, experimentation, feedback synthesis, analytics. From «PM manually gathers insights» — to «AI does synthesis, PM thinks strategically».
ai-native-product.why: Product management is the most «strategic-thinking» role in the company. AI handles routine work (interview synthesis, spec writing, feedback reading), freeing the PM for high-value work: prioritization, vision, stakeholder alignment.
ai-native-product.when: When the PM spends ≥30% of time on manual synthesis (interviews, feedback, data). When the team loses insights between tickets/Slack/calls. When the discovery → ship cycle is slow because of «need to write a PRD».
ai-native-product.impact: 7 nodes cover the full product lifecycle: discovery (research) → definition (spec) → planning (roadmap) → experimentation → measurement (analytics) + sense-making (feedback) + team operating model.
ai-native-product.example:
Maturity stages for Product:
Stage 0: Pre-AI — manual research, gut prioritization, long PRD writing.
Stage 1: AI experiments — Claude helps write individual PRDs.
Stage 2: AI workflows — Project with research patterns, AI does primary synthesis.
Stage 3: AI-native — PM as conductor: AI does discovery/synthesis/specs, PM does strategy.
Stage 4: AI-first — products with AI capabilities as core feature, not add-on.
ai-native-product.mistakes: Thinking AI will replace product judgment. AI is good at synthesis and pattern matching, but prioritization requires business context, stakeholder politics, market intuition. AI = co-pilot, PM remains pilot.

pd-discovery-research.title: AI Discovery Research
pd-discovery-research.what: AI-powered user research: automatic interview synthesis, competitive analysis, market research. From «read 20 interviews in 3 days» — to «AI extracts themes in an hour, PM validates».
pd-discovery-research.why: Discovery is the most time-intensive part of PM work. 50 interviews = a week of manual synthesis. AI does a first pass in an hour, the PM focuses on validation and interpretation.
pd-discovery-research.when: When there are >10 interviews/customer calls on one topic. When quarterly customer research is needed. When the competitive landscape changes and you need to track it.
pd-discovery-research.impact: Time-to-insight: days → hours. Coverage: PM can «process» 50 interviews instead of 10. Quality: structured themes instead of «here are my notes». Stage 1→2.
pd-discovery-research.example:
Research Synthesis Workflow:

  Inputs:
  - 30 interview transcripts
  - Customer support tickets (1 month)
  - Competitor reviews on G2/Trustpilot
        ↓
  Project «Research» with RAG index
        ↓
  AI Steps:
  1. Extract themes (frequency + sentiment)
  2. Cluster similar quotes
  3. Identify gaps (what people often mention but we do not do)
  4. Generate hypothesis matrix
        ↓
  PM validates: which themes are actionable, which need follow-up
        ↓
  Output: structured research report + raw data accessible

Metric: time-to-insight, theme coverage.
pd-discovery-research.mistakes: Relying on AI without human validation. AI misses nuance: irony, edge cases, cultural context. Workflow: AI extracts → PM validates a 10-20% sample → confidence in the rest grows. Without validation — false insights.

pd-spec-generation.title: AI Spec Generation
pd-spec-generation.what: AI writes PRDs, user stories, technical specs from a rough idea + research input. From «PM sits for 2 days writing a PRD» — to «PM iterates with AI for 2 hours, draft is ready».
pd-spec-generation.why: PRD writing is a shipping bottleneck. PMs spend days formatting/structuring what they already know in their heads. AI handles the «writing» part, the PM focuses on content quality.
pd-spec-generation.when: When the team loses momentum between «have an idea» and «PRD written». When there is a documented PRD template. When rough notes / research are already on hand.
pd-spec-generation.impact: Time-to-PRD: 2 days → 4 hours (including iterations). Consistency: a single format for all specs. Quality: AI catches missing sections (success metrics, edge cases, etc.). Stage 1→2.
pd-spec-generation.example:
Spec Generation Workflow:

  Input for AI:
  - Rough idea (3-5 sentences from PM)
  - Research output (from pd-discovery)
  - Existing PRD template + 2-3 high-quality examples
        ↓
  AI generates:
  - Problem statement
  - User stories with acceptance criteria
  - Success metrics proposals
  - Open questions
  - Technical considerations (for engineering)
        ↓
  PM iterates: 3-5 rounds of edits
        ↓
  Output: ship-ready PRD

Metric: time-to-spec, dev team feedback on PRD quality.
pd-spec-generation.mistakes: Doing AI-PRDs without research input. «Write a PRD for feature X» = generic stuff. Quality output requires quality input: research, examples, constraints. Garbage in = garbage out.

pd-roadmap-intelligence.title: AI Roadmap Intelligence
pd-roadmap-intelligence.what: AI helps with roadmap prioritization: analyzing feedback patterns, competitor moves, customer requests, internal data → ranked priorities with reasoning. AI = «second analyst» in roadmap discussions.
pd-roadmap-intelligence.why: Roadmap prioritization is usually done «by gut» under stakeholder pressure. AI brings a structured framework: explicit weights, data-based scoring, consideration of alternatives.
pd-roadmap-intelligence.when: Quarterly planning. Before a roadmap review with executives. When «everyone has their own opinion» and a structured framework is needed for the decision.
pd-roadmap-intelligence.impact: Reactive prioritization: -60%. Stakeholder alignment: faster (data, not opinions). Roadmap thrashing: reduced (explicit criteria prevent frequent changes). Stage 2→3.
pd-roadmap-intelligence.example:
Roadmap Prioritization Workflow:

  Inputs:
  - All product opportunities (backlog + new ideas)
  - Customer feedback themes (from feedback-synthesis)
  - Competitor analysis
  - Internal metrics (revenue impact, retention)
  - Strategic objectives (current quarter)
        ↓
  AI Scoring:
  - Each opportunity rated on: impact, effort, strategic fit, risk
  - Reasoning explicit for each
  - Alternative orderings played out
        ↓
  PM + leadership: review AI ranking + override based on judgment
        ↓
  Output: prioritized roadmap with documented reasoning

Value: next quarter you CAN explain «why we chose this».
pd-roadmap-intelligence.mistakes: Accepting AI roadmap as final. AI scoring is based on the data you gave — but it does not know board politics, executive priorities, or upcoming launches. AI = input into a decision, not the decision itself.

pd-experimentation.title: AI Feature Experimentation
pd-experimentation.what: AI support for A/B testing: hypothesis generation, variant design, statistical analysis interpretation, learnings synthesis. From «ran A/B, forgot results» — to «structured experimentation engine».
pd-experimentation.why: Most teams run A/B tests poorly: weak hypotheses, no power analysis, results forgotten. AI structures this: forces explicit hypothesis, generates variant ideas, helps interpret results.
pd-experimentation.when: When the team runs ≥3 experiments per quarter. When experiment outputs do not turn into product knowledge. When you need to scale experimentation across multiple teams.
pd-experimentation.impact: Experiment velocity: +50%. Experiments with clear learnings: 50% → 90%. Knowledge retention: structured library of experiment outcomes. Stage 2→3.
pd-experimentation.example:
Experimentation Workflow:

  1. Hypothesis Generation:
     - PM inputs: «hypothesis: shorter onboarding → higher activation»
     - AI critiques: «specify metric, magnitude, timeframe, sample needed»
     - Result: «If we cut onboarding from 5 to 2 steps, activation rate +15% over 4 weeks (n>1000)»

  2. Variant Design:
     - AI generates 3-5 specific variant approaches
     - Discusses pros/cons of each

  3. Post-experiment Analysis:
     - Input: results data
     - AI: «winner with X confidence. Caveats: ... Recommended follow-up: ...»

  4. Library:
     - AI maintains experiment knowledge base
     - Search: «did we try X before?»

Metric: experiments per quarter, learnings library size.
pd-experimentation.mistakes: Using AI for «predict before run». AI cannot predict the result of an A/B (if it could — an A/B would not be needed). AI is good at: hypothesis sharpening, variant ideation, post-analysis interpretation. Not predictive.

pd-feedback-synthesis.title: AI Feedback Synthesis
pd-feedback-synthesis.what: AI reads all user feedback (NPS comments, support tickets, reviews, sales notes) → structured insights with trends. From «PM read ~50 comments» — to «AI processed 5000 and found patterns».
pd-feedback-synthesis.why: Customer feedback is fragmented across 5-10 sources. The PM physically cannot read everything. AI does aggregation + synthesis. Sentiment shifts visible before they show up in churn.
pd-feedback-synthesis.when: When there are ≥3 feedback sources (NPS, support, reviews, sales calls, social). When the product team wants «voice of customer» systematic, not anecdotal.
pd-feedback-synthesis.impact: Coverage: 5% of feedback is read → 100% is processed. Time-to-trend: 2 months → 2 weeks. Decision quality: data-backed instead of «I remember someone complained». Stage 2→3.
pd-feedback-synthesis.example:
Feedback Synthesis Pipeline:

  Sources (weekly):
  - NPS responses (quarterly × 1000+)
  - Support tickets with CSAT comments
  - App store / G2 reviews
  - Sales call notes
  - Social mentions
        ↓
  AI Processing:
  1. Clean + deduplicate
  2. Categorize (feature, UX, pricing, performance, ...)
  3. Sentiment analysis
  4. Theme extraction
  5. Trend detection (what changed week-over-week)
        ↓
  Weekly Output:
  - Top 5 themes (with magnitude + delta)
  - Quote samples for each
  - Critical issues to investigate
        ↓
  Distribution:
  - Product team review (decisions)
  - Engineering: bug themes
  - Marketing: positioning themes

Metric: feedback coverage, time-to-action on trending issues.
pd-feedback-synthesis.mistakes: Doing feedback synthesis in a vacuum. Output must flow into roadmap planning, not into a read-only report. Workflow: synthesis → product review → roadmap update → measure impact. Without the loop — polite theater.

pd-product-analytics.title: AI Product Analytics
pd-product-analytics.what: AI reads product usage data (Amplitude, Mixpanel, GA) → writes insight reports with hypotheses «why did this happen?» and suggested investigations. From «here is a dashboard» — to «here is what happened and what it means».
pd-product-analytics.why: Product analytics tools show «what happened», but not «why». PM/analytics manager spends hours on formulating hypotheses. AI does this first-pass, the human verifies.
pd-product-analytics.when: Weekly product reviews. After every major release. When a metric is unexpected (growth or drop). When the team «does not understand why» something is happening.
pd-product-analytics.impact: Time-to-hypothesis: days → hours. Coverage: analytics-aware decisions grow from 30% to 70%+ of the team. Stage 2→3.
pd-product-analytics.example:
Weekly Product Analytics Workflow:

  Inputs:
  - Top-line metrics (DAU, MAU, retention, activation)
  - Feature usage (new + existing)
  - User segments behavior
  - Recent product releases
        ↓
  AI Analysis:
  1. What changed (numbers + delta + significance)
  2. Correlation: «release X → metric Y +Z%»
  3. Anomaly detection (unusual segment behavior)
  4. Hypotheses (ranked by likelihood)
  5. Recommended investigations (queries to run, segments to look at)
        ↓
  Product team:
  - Validates top hypotheses
  - Decides actions
  - Adds learnings to knowledge base

Metric: % of metric changes with documented explanation.
pd-product-analytics.mistakes: Trusting AI causal claims. «Release X caused metric Y +5%» — that is correlation, not causation. AI recommends a hypothesis, the human must validate via proper analysis (cohort, A/B, before-after).

pd-team-workflow.title: AI Product Team Workflow
pd-team-workflow.what: Product team operating model with AI: shared research workspace, common spec templates, feedback synthesis pipeline, weekly AI office hours. From «every PM with their own Claude» — to a «collaborative AI-powered product team».
pd-team-workflow.why: Individual usage in product does not scale — research findings are lost between PMs, specs are inconsistent, knowledge is not shared. Team workflow creates a shared institutional memory.
pd-team-workflow.when: Product team ≥3 PMs use AI. When «everyone has their own approach to specs». When research findings are lost after launch. When a new PM «does not know how we work».
pd-team-workflow.impact: Team velocity: +30%. New PM onboarding: 6 weeks → 3 weeks (via shared knowledge). Decision quality: improves over time (institutional memory grows). Stage 2→3.
pd-team-workflow.example:
Product Team Setup:

1. Shared Claude Project «Product Workspace»:
   - All research transcripts indexed
   - Past PRDs library
   - Experiment learnings
   - Customer feedback (categorized)

2. CLAUDE.md: writing conventions, PRD template, decision frameworks.

3. Skills:
   - research-synthesizer
   - prd-drafter
   - feedback-categorizer
   - experiment-designer

4. Weekly «AI office hours» 30 min:
   - Best prompt discoveries
   - Failed AI experiments (what is not working)
   - Cross-team learning

5. Quarterly knowledge curation:
   - What to add to shared workspace
   - What is outdated and to remove

Stage 3 sign: new PM writes a shipping-ready PRD by the end of the first month.
pd-team-workflow.mistakes: Doing team workflow without a librarian role. Shared workspace without maintainership = junk drawer in 6 months. Someone must curate: weekly review of new content, monthly cleanup of outdated.

uc-ai-discovery-launch.title: Use Case: Launch AI Discovery in 2 Weeks
uc-ai-discovery-launch.what: Full path from «doing research by hand» to «AI-powered discovery pipeline». Cross-layer path through 6 nodes: Foundation → Systems → Transformation.
uc-ai-discovery-launch.why: The most common product team request: «we have tons of interviews / feedback / research, but synthesis is a bottleneck». This UC solves it systematically via RAG + workflows + product practices.
uc-ai-discovery-launch.when: When the product team has ≥30 interviews or ≥100 feedback items without structured processing. When the discovery → ship cycle is slow. When there is buy-in from Head of Product.
uc-ai-discovery-launch.impact: Outcome: working AI-discovery pipeline in 2 weeks. Metrics: time-to-insight ≤2 hours per topic, research coverage 100% (vs 30% manually), structured theme extraction.
uc-ai-discovery-launch.example:
Path (6 steps):

Week 1: Setup foundation.
1. Foundation: prompting → how to formulate synthesis prompts
2. Foundation: af-rag-basics → RAG basics for research repository
3. Foundation: projects → create «Discovery Workspace» with research files

Week 1-2: Build pipeline.
4. Systems: sys-context-passing → properly pass research context between steps
5. Transformation: pd-discovery-research → concrete workflow with PM validation gates

Week 2: Extend & sustain.
6. Transformation: pd-feedback-synthesis → extend to ongoing feedback (not just interviews)

Day 1-3: Index existing research in the Project. Test synthesis on 5-10 interviews.
Day 4-7: Refine prompts based on validation feedback. Document patterns.
Day 8-14: Scale to the full research backlog. Train other PMs.

Stage transition: 1→2.
uc-ai-discovery-launch.mistakes: Doing a UC without structured research input. If interviews are scattered chaotically across Notion / Google Docs / Slack — AI cannot find them. Day 1 work = organize the research repository. This is 30% of UC time. Do not skip.

ai-native-enterprise.title: AI-Native Enterprise
ai-native-enterprise.what: Strategic layer of AI transformation: transformation strategy, change management, governance, Center of Excellence, ROI measurement, risk management, talent strategy. For CIO/CTO/Head of AI: how an organization becomes AI-native as a whole.
ai-native-enterprise.why: All other Transformation directions (Operations/Marketing/Support/Product) are tactical. Without an enterprise layer, they remain «islands of AI». Enterprise = connective tissue: governance, ROI logic, talent pipeline, change framework.
ai-native-enterprise.when: Company invests in AI at the strategy level (not isolated pilots). An AI lead role emerges. The board asks questions about AI ROI. You need to coordinate 3+ tactical AI initiatives.
ai-native-enterprise.impact: All tactical AI initiatives become a coherent program. Strategic decisions backed by data (ROI). Risk and governance — not an afterthought, but built-in. Stage 2→4 over a year.
ai-native-enterprise.example:
Maturity stages for Enterprise:
Stage 0: Pre-AI — no AI strategy, isolated pilots without coordination.
Stage 1: Ad-hoc — 1-2 successful AI use cases, no org-wide approach.
Stage 2: Strategic — AI strategy doc exists, CoE started, main roles defined.
Stage 3: Org-wide — all 4 tactical directions running, ROI measured, governance in place.
Stage 4: AI-first — business model + products built on AI capabilities, AI = competitive advantage.
ai-native-enterprise.mistakes: Doing Enterprise AI as a top-down directive. AI transformation requires bottom-up adoption + top-down structure. Structure only — pilots will not launch. Pilots only — fragmentation and burnout. Need both.

en-transformation-strategy.title: AI Transformation Strategy
en-transformation-strategy.what: A document-based AI strategy for 12-24 months: vision, north-star metrics, sequencing of initiatives, investment thesis, success criteria. Not «let us use AI», but «here is HOW we win from AI».
en-transformation-strategy.why: Without explicit strategy, AI initiatives = different departments doing different things. With strategy — coordination, leverage between departments, clear priorities. Strategy doc = alignment tool for leadership.
en-transformation-strategy.when: After 6-12 months of successful pilots in several departments. When the board asks questions about AI ROI. Before annual planning. When you need to hire an AI lead.
en-transformation-strategy.impact: Decision velocity: 3× faster on AI-related decisions. Org alignment: leadership team on the same page (literally). Time-to-execution: tactical teams understand priorities in days, not months. Stage 2→3.
en-transformation-strategy.example:
AI Transformation Strategy doc (8-12 pages):

1. Vision (1 page): where the company is in 2 years with AI
2. North-star metrics (3-5): cost reduction, revenue growth, NPS, talent retention
3. Strategic bets (3-7): «Stage-by-stage AI in customer support», «AI-augmented product development», ...
4. Sequencing: what we do Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4
5. Investment thesis: where we spend, where we save
6. Risk & governance principles
7. Success criteria + checkpoints

Creation process: 2-3 weeks with executives + tactical leads. Reviewed quarterly.

Metric: % of strategic decisions referencing the doc (target: >80% in 6 months).
en-transformation-strategy.mistakes: Making a strategy doc «once and forgotten». The AI landscape changes every 6 months — the strategy must refresh quarterly. And: not making just vision without metrics. Strategy without measurable outcomes = wish list.

en-change-management.title: AI Change Management
en-change-management.what: Structured approach to changing team behaviors under AI-native operations: communication, training, role evolution, resistance management. Tech adoption ≠ change management — these are different disciplines.
en-change-management.why: The most common cause of failed AI initiatives is not tech, but adoption. Teams fear (job loss), do not believe (saw hype before), do not know (skills gap). Change management addresses this explicitly.
en-change-management.when: Before rolling out a tactical direction to the full team. When the first pilots work but adoption stalls. When there is an «AI champions» vs «AI skeptics» split on the team.
en-change-management.impact: Adoption rate: 30% → 80% with proper change mgmt. Resistance reduced (not eliminated). Skills gap closes via structured training. Time-to-Stage 3: -50% for tactical directions.
en-change-management.example:
Change Management Framework (for one tactical direction):

Phase 1: Awareness (week 1-2)
  - All-hands: «here is what we are doing + why»
  - Q&A sessions: address concerns openly
  - Champions identification

Phase 2: Education (week 3-4)
  - Hands-on workshops for everyone
  - Skill development: 10 hours of structured learning
  - Champions trained deeper

Phase 3: Adoption (week 5-12)
  - Pilot teams using daily
  - Office hours for help
  - Wins shared widely

Phase 4: Reinforcement (ongoing)
  - Promotion criteria include AI usage
  - Career path for «AI-augmented» roles
  - Continuous learning culture

Metric: % of team actively using AI weekly.
en-change-management.mistakes: Thinking that training = change management. Training is skill transfer. Change mgmt is behavioral shift. Without the second, the first = waste. And: not answering «will I lose my job?». Avoiding it = doubt grows.

en-governance.title: AI Governance
en-governance.what: Set of rules and processes governing how AI is used in the organization: data privacy, model selection, output validation, vendor management, compliance. Not «security team forbids» — but «structured framework for responsible use».
en-governance.why: Without governance, compliance gaps accumulate: data leaks via AI inputs, customer data in third-party models, audit trail missing. Regulatory landscape (GDPR, EU AI Act) tightens — better get ahead.
en-governance.when: Before production AI use cases (NOT after). When there is customer data, financial data, PII in AI flows. When multiple departments use different AI tools.
en-governance.impact: Compliance: prevented incidents. Trust: customers trust AI products. Speed: clear rules speed up decision-making (no «can we or can we not?» discussions). Risk reduction quantifiable.
en-governance.example:
AI Governance Framework:

1. Data classification: what can/cannot go into AI flows
   - Public data: any AI tool
   - Internal data: approved enterprise tools only
   - Customer data: with consent + data residency check
   - PII: encrypted + DPA in place

2. Vendor management:
   - Approved AI tools list (updated quarterly)
   - DPA requirements
   - Audit logs

3. Output validation:
   - Human review for customer-facing AI outputs
   - Quality monitoring (statistical)
   - Bias testing

4. Incident response:
   - AI-specific incident playbook
   - Reporting channels

Reviewed: quarterly + after any incident.

Metric: incidents per quarter (target: 0 high-severity).
en-governance.mistakes: Doing governance as a «list of prohibitions». Governance works as an enabler if framed as «here is how to do this responsibly». Without enablement framing — shadow AI usage (teams use unauthorized tools).

en-coe.title: AI Center of Excellence
en-coe.what: Central team (3-10 people) — AI lead, ML engineers, AI ethicists, product manager — supporting tactical teams: best practices, shared infrastructure, training, governance liaison. Not building everything, but enabling others.
en-coe.why: Without a CoE, each tactical team reinvents the wheel: discovers RAG, learns prompt engineering, sets up vector DB. CoE shares this knowledge and infrastructure → 5-10× faster for all subsequent teams.
en-coe.when: After 2-3 successful tactical AI directions. When «how and where do I find an AI expert?» becomes a regular question. When signing up for enterprise AI vendors (CoE manages).
en-coe.impact: New AI initiative time-to-launch: 6 months → 2 months. Cost: shared infra cheaper than per-team setup. Quality: best practices spread. Career: clear AI path for talent.
en-coe.example:
CoE Structure:

Core team (3-5):
  - Head of AI / Chief AI Officer
  - Senior ML/AI engineer
  - AI Product Manager
  - AI Ethics & Governance lead

Functions:
  1. Shared infrastructure (vector DBs, LLM API contracts, monitoring)
  2. Best practices library (CLAUDE.md templates, Skills, patterns)
  3. Office hours (weekly, anyone can attend)
  4. Training programs (3 levels: foundational, intermediate, advanced)
  5. Tooling decisions (which AI tools company-wide)
  6. Governance coordination (with security/legal)
  7. Talent: hiring AI roles + upskilling existing
  8. Showcase: monthly «AI demos» across the company

Key metric: CoE-enabled launches per quarter.
en-coe.mistakes: Making CoE «the AI department» — building everything. CoE = enablement, not execution. Tactical teams build, CoE shares know-how. Otherwise CoE becomes a bottleneck.

en-roi-measurement.title: AI ROI Measurement
en-roi-measurement.what: Framework for measuring AI investment returns: cost vs value, attribution to AI vs other factors, leading vs lagging indicators, payback period. Turns «AI saves time» into «AI saved $X this quarter».
en-roi-measurement.why: Without ROI measurement, AI initiatives ride on vibes. When finance asks «show me the money?», the response should be quantified. ROI measurement = sustainable AI program longevity.
en-roi-measurement.when: After 3-6 months of AI in production. Before budget planning (annual or quarterly). When executives ask about AI value. When you need to prioritize between AI initiatives.
en-roi-measurement.impact: Budget approval: 2× faster for AI initiatives with tracked ROI. Resource allocation: efficient (kill failing, double on winning). Stakeholder confidence: high. Stage 2→3.
en-roi-measurement.example:
AI ROI Framework:

Cost side:
  - Direct: AI API costs, tools, infrastructure
  - Indirect: training time, change management, governance overhead
  - Hidden: opportunity cost of team time

Value side:
  - Time saved (× hourly cost of saved roles)
  - Quality improvement (cost of errors avoided)
  - Revenue generated (new capabilities)
  - Risk reduction (compliance, incidents avoided)
  - Customer satisfaction (retention impact)

Attribution: how to know AI caused this?
  - Before/after comparison + control group when possible
  - A/B testing on features
  - Counterfactual analysis for high-stakes claims

Reporting:
  - Monthly per tactical direction
  - Quarterly aggregate to leadership
  - Annual: full impact report

Metric: documented ROI per initiative > 3× cost (target).
en-roi-measurement.mistakes: Counting only cost savings, ignoring intangibles. AI brings not only time — but capability gains, morale, future optionality. Without holistic ROI — value undervalued, program cancelled prematurely.

en-risk-management.title: AI Risk Management
en-risk-management.what: Systematic identification, assessment, mitigation of AI-specific risks: hallucinations in production, model drift, data leaks, regulatory non-compliance, bias, vendor dependencies. Risk awareness, not risk avoidance.
en-risk-management.why: AI risks differ from traditional IT risks: probabilistic, evolving, often invisible until late. Traditional risk frameworks do not catch them. Need an AI-specific approach.
en-risk-management.when: From day 1 of every AI initiative (NOT after an incident). Before production launch. Annually for existing AI systems. After any notable industry incident.
en-risk-management.impact: High-severity incidents: 0 prevented to occurred (best outcome). Insurance cost: lower with documented program. Regulatory readiness: ahead of EU AI Act, NIST framework. Stage 2→3.
en-risk-management.example:
AI Risk Categories + Mitigations:

1. Hallucinations:
   - Risk: AI returns wrong info confidently
   - Mitigation: RAG with citations, human review for customer-facing, quality monitoring

2. Model drift:
   - Risk: AI behavior changes without notice (model update, data shift)
   - Mitigation: continuous quality monitoring, golden test sets, rollback ability

3. Data leaks:
   - Risk: customer/sensitive data in model providers
   - Mitigation: data classification, approved vendors, encryption, audit logs

4. Bias:
   - Risk: AI discriminates (hiring, pricing, content)
   - Mitigation: bias testing, diverse training data, monitoring by demographic

5. Regulatory:
   - Risk: GDPR, EU AI Act, sector-specific violations
   - Mitigation: compliance review per use case, legal sign-off, documentation

6. Vendor lock:
   - Risk: depends entirely on one AI provider
   - Mitigation: abstraction layer, multi-vendor strategy, internal fallback

Risk register: updated quarterly.

Metric: identified vs occurred risks (catch rate target: >90%).
en-risk-management.mistakes: Thinking risk management = compliance checklist. Real AI risk management = thinking about edge cases, scenarios, second-order effects. Checklist alone — false security.

en-talent-strategy.title: AI Talent Strategy
en-talent-strategy.what: Approach to building AI capability on the team: hiring AI roles, upskilling existing employees, retention in the AI-talent market, career paths for AI-augmented roles. Talent is the hardest part for long-term AI success.
en-talent-strategy.why: AI tools are commodity, AI talent is not. Companies without a talent strategy lose people to Big Tech. Companies with a good strategy attract top talent, retain existing employees via growth opportunities.
en-talent-strategy.when: Continuously (not «one time»). Before every tactical direction launch. When scaling the AI program. When attrition in AI-relevant roles rises.
en-talent-strategy.impact: AI talent retention: 90%+ (vs 60% industry average). Time-to-fill AI roles: 2× faster (employer brand). Internal mobility: 30%+ move into AI-augmented roles. Stage 2→3.
en-talent-strategy.example:
AI Talent Strategy:

1. Hiring framework:
   - Roles needed: ML engineers, AI PMs, AI ethicists, prompt engineers
   - Compensation benchmarks (AI talent premium)
   - Sourcing channels (universities, conferences, community)

2. Upskilling:
   - 3 levels: foundational (everyone), intermediate (heavy users), advanced (builders)
   - Time budget: 4-8 hours/month protected learning time
   - Recognition: AI skills in performance reviews

3. Career paths:
   - «AI-augmented» version of every role (e.g., AI-augmented PM, AI-augmented designer)
   - New roles: AI ops, AI product, prompt engineer
   - Senior path for AI builders

4. Retention:
   - AI projects = career capital (assignment to AI work seen as opportunity)
   - Internal mobility: skill-based moves to AI-heavy teams
   - External brand: conference talks, blog posts, GitHub

5. Culture:
   - «AI-curious» as core value
   - Failed AI experiments celebrated (learning culture)
   - Cross-team AI showcases

Metric: AI skills inventory (% of workforce with documented AI proficiency).
en-talent-strategy.mistakes: Hiring ML engineers and thinking talent strategy is done. They build, but do not replace product, marketing, support skill needs. AI talent strategy = broad upskilling + targeted hiring. Not one or the other.

uc-ai-transformation-roadmap.title: Use Case: Enterprise AI Transformation Roadmap
uc-ai-transformation-roadmap.what: Full path from «doing AI pilots ad-hoc» to «AI-native company-wide operations». Cross-layer + cross-direction path: enterprise strategy → tactical roll-outs → org-wide change. 6-12 months of work.
uc-ai-transformation-roadmap.why: This is the highest-level UC in Atlas — for CEO/CIO/Head of AI. Shows how a company systematically does AI transformation across ALL departments at once with governance + measurement.
uc-ai-transformation-roadmap.when: When the company commits to AI transformation strategically (not isolated pilots). When there is executive buy-in. When there is resource commitment ($M+ budget) for 12-24 months.
uc-ai-transformation-roadmap.impact: Outcome: company at Stage 3 AI-native operations in 12 months. Metrics: 4+ tactical directions running, $X ROI documented, governance in place, 80%+ team AI-proficient.
uc-ai-transformation-roadmap.example:
Roadmap (12 months):

Q1 (Foundation):
1. Enterprise: en-transformation-strategy → write strategy doc
2. Enterprise: en-coe → form CoE team (3-5 people)
3. Enterprise: en-governance → governance framework
4. Select first 2 tactical pilots: ai-native-customer-support OR ai-native-operations

Q2 (Tactical Pilots):
5. Launch tactical pilot #1 (highest ROI: usually Support tier-1)
6. Launch tactical pilot #2 (most strategic: usually Product or Marketing)
7. Enterprise: en-change-management → start change program
8. Enterprise: en-talent-strategy → AI upskilling roll-out

Q3 (Scale):
9. Add tactical direction #3 (based on Q2 learnings)
10. Enterprise: en-roi-measurement → measure first 6 months impact
11. Enterprise: en-risk-management → formal risk register
12. CoE → share best practices org-wide

Q4 (Maturity):
13. Add tactical direction #4 (full 4 directions running)
14. Strategy refresh based on learnings
15. Annual report to board: ROI, capabilities, risks

Stage transition: Stage 1→3 in 12 months (realistic).
Stage 4 — next 12-18 months.
uc-ai-transformation-roadmap.mistakes: Launching all 4 tactical directions in parallel in Q1. That is a recipe for chaos and burnout. Sequential: 1 in Q1, 2 in Q2, 3 in Q3, 4 in Q4. Each previous teaches the organization. Do not try «AI everything overnight».
